name: Tibetan multiphonic yang chant
lineage: Tibetan Buddhist monastic multiphonic yang chant tradition of the Gelug-school tantric colleges Gyuto and Gyume (founded 1474 and 1485, respectively, by Sherab Sengge, a direct disciple of Tsongkhapa). The yang chant technique produces a chest-register-pitched fundamental enriched with audible upper-partial overtones such that a single voice produces what sounds like a chord — the third, fifth, and sometimes higher partials being amplified into clearly audible voice-leading register. Multiple monks chanting in unison produce a thick texture of fundamental-plus-overtones across the assembly. Repertoire centers on the Lama Chöpa (Guru Puja), the Yamantaka tantric cycles, the Guhyasamaja tantric cycles, and the Chakrasamvara tantric cycles. Accompaniment by the canonical monastic-ensemble percussion: rolmo large paired cymbals, dril-bu small hand-bell, damaru double-headed hand-drum, dung-chen long telescoping copper-or-brass trumpet (the four-meter-long ceremonial instrument, played in pairs, capable of producing the very-low subharmonic that anchors the ensemble), rgya-gling double-reed oboe (the melodic-leading instrument when wind voices are present), and kangling thigh-bone trumpet (for specific wrathful-deity cycles). Huston Smith's 1967 Music of Tibet recordings (GemsTone GT1003-CD reissue 2005) and David Lewiston's 1971 Nonesuch Explorer H-72071 Tibetan Ritual Music constitute the principal Western-distributed documentation. Distinguished from Mongolian khoomei by Tibetan yang chant's ensemble (vs solo) and liturgical (vs secular) framework; distinguished from Sakya-school chant by Gelug-specific tantric-cycle repertoire; distinguished from Bön pre-Buddhist Tibetan chant by Buddhist tantric-text base.
